# Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation

Day 2, 14:15 · Google · coverage: transcript, slides

## Claims

- **[Stage]** Google may find a site's different language versions on its own, without the site owner doing anything, but owners can take steps to make this easier for Google.
  <br><sub>`D2-C559` · Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation (Google) · confirmed by Google docs · [Tell Google about localized versions of your page](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/localized-versions)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Each language version should have its own URL; switching languages with cookies or by updating the content in place makes the versions very difficult for Google to handle.
  <br><sub>`D2-C560` · Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation (Google) · confirmed by Google docs · [Managing multi-regional and multilingual sites](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/managing-multi-regional-sites), [How Google crawls locale-adaptive pages](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/locale-adaptive-pages) · Used by `DEV-INT-01`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's documentation says Googlebot mostly crawls from US IP addresses and sends no Accept-Language header, so pages that change content or redirect by the visitor's perceived country or language may not have every version crawled, indexed or ranked; it recommends separate URLs annotated with hreflang.
  <br><sub>`D2-C561` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation · is the documentation · [How Google crawls locale-adaptive pages](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/locale-adaptive-pages), [Managing multi-regional and multilingual sites](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/managing-multi-regional-sites) · Used by `DEV-INT-01`, `DEV-INT-02`</sub>

- **[Slide]** Language versions can also be language-plus-region variants: Google's example site had a generic English page (en), a UK English page (en-gb) and a Spanish page (es), each on its own URL.
  <br><sub>`D2-C562` · Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation (Google) · confirmed by Google docs · [Tell Google about localized versions of your page](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/localized-versions) · Extended by [D2-C627](D2-S16-lightning-session-g-internationalisation.md) · Used by `DEV-INT-01`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's hreflang guide says language-specific subdomains such as en, en-gb or de in a URL are not used to determine a page's target audience; site owners must map the audience explicitly, for example with hreflang.
  <br><sub>`D2-C563` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation · is the documentation · [Tell Google about localized versions of your page](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/localized-versions)</sub>

- **[Slide]** Google's hreflang example lists every language version in the page's HTML head as a link element with rel=alternate, the version's full URL and its hreflang code (en, en-gb, es), including the page's own URL.
  <br><sub>`D2-C564` · Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation (Google) · confirmed by Google docs · [Tell Google about localized versions of your page](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/localized-versions) · Used by `DEV-INT-03`, the glossary term *hreflang*</sub>

- **[Slide]** Missing return links are a common hreflang mistake: if page X names page Y as a language version, page Y must link back to page X.
  > "If page X links to page Y, page Y must link back to page X."
  <br><sub>`D2-C565` · Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation (Google) · confirmed by Google docs · [Tell Google about localized versions of your page](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/localized-versions) · Used by `DEV-INT-03`, the glossary term *hreflang return link*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Each page in an hreflang set must also list its own URL, and a missing self-reference is a common mistake Google sees.
  <br><sub>`D2-C566` · Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [Tell Google about localized versions of your page](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/localized-versions) · Used by `DEV-INT-03`</sub>

- **[Stage]** When the HTML head is not suitable for a page, hreflang can be given by other methods instead, such as listing the language versions in a sitemap.
  <br><sub>`D2-C567` · Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation (Google) · confirmed by Google docs · [Tell Google about localized versions of your page](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/localized-versions) · Used by `DEV-INT-05`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Any one hreflang method is fine, but a site should use only one: Google often sees sites using two or three methods at the same time, with annotations that conflict.
  <br><sub>`D2-C568` · Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [Tell Google about localized versions of your page](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/localized-versions) · Used by `DEV-INT-05`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's hreflang guide says its three methods (link elements in the HTML head, an HTTP Link header, which suits non-HTML files such as PDFs, and an XML sitemap) are equivalent; using several at once is allowed but brings no benefit in Search and is harder to manage.
  <br><sub>`D2-C569` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation · is the documentation · [Tell Google about localized versions of your page](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/localized-versions) · Used by `DEV-INT-05`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google ignores hreflang annotations that point only one way, where page A names page B as a language version but page B does not name page A back.
  <br><sub>`D2-C570` · Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation (Google) · confirmed by Google docs · [Tell Google about localized versions of your page](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/localized-versions) · Used by `DEV-INT-03`, the glossary term *hreflang return link*</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's hreflang guide says a site that finds it hard to keep every language pair bidirectional may omit some languages on some pages, because Google still processes the pairs that point to each other; new language versions should at least link both ways with the original or dominant language.
  <br><sub>`D2-C571` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation · is the documentation · [Tell Google about localized versions of your page](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/localized-versions) · Used by `DEV-INT-03`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google requires hreflang return links because an alternate URL is a full URL that can be on any domain, so without them any site could declare itself a language version of someone else's website.
  <br><sub>`D2-C572` · Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation (Google) · confirmed by Google docs · [Tell Google about localized versions of your page](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/localized-versions) · Used by `DEV-INT-03`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's hreflang guide says alternate URLs must be fully qualified, including the protocol (https://example.com/foo, not //example.com/foo or /foo), and need not be on the same domain.
  <br><sub>`D2-C573` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation · is the documentation · [Tell Google about localized versions of your page](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/localized-versions) · Used by `DEV-INT-03`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Audit hreflang per cluster rather than per page: check that every page lists itself and all its alternates, that every alternate links back, and that only one method (HTML head, HTTP header or sitemap) supplies the annotations.
  <br><sub>`D2-C574` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation · Used by `DEV-INT-03`</sub>

  <br><sub>`D2-C575` · Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [Tell Google about localized versions of your page](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/localized-versions) · Extended by [D2-C962](D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) · Used by `DEV-INT-04`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Site owners do not need to memorise hreflang language and region codes, but should double-check every code when implementing hreflang.

  <br><sub>`D2-C578` · Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [Tell Google about localized versions of your page](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/localized-versions) · Used by `DEV-INT-04`</sub>

- **[Slide]** hreflang region codes must be ISO 3166-1 Alpha-2 country codes; frequent mistakes are UK instead of GB for the United Kingdom, SW instead of CH for Switzerland and GE instead of DE for Germany.
  <br><sub>`D2-C579` · Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [Tell Google about localized versions of your page](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/localized-versions) · Used by `DEV-INT-04`</sub>

- **[Slide]** EU is not a valid hreflang region code: sites use it hoping to target the European Union, but hreflang targeting works only by country.
  <br><sub>`D2-C580` · Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation (Google) · confirmed by Google docs · [Tell Google about localized versions of your page](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/localized-versions) · Used by `DEV-INT-04`</sub>

- **[Slide]** Google also flagged LA used as a region code for Los Angeles (a city, not a country) and SA used for South Africa as wrong hreflang region codes.

- **[Slide]** A region code cannot be used on its own in hreflang: en and en-GB are valid values, but GB alone is not, because the value must name a language.

- **[Analysis]** Validate hreflang values against the ISO 639-1 and ISO 3166-1 Alpha-2 lists in a crawler rule or build check rather than by eye: reserved codes such as UK and EU are simply ignored, but some plausible mistakes are valid codes for something else (se is Northern Sami, GE Georgia, LA Laos, SA Saudi Arabia) and silently point the annotation at the wrong audience.

- **[Stage]** Google does not use hreflang to determine a page's language when indexing the page.
  <br><sub>`D2-C584` · Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation (Google) · confirmed by Google docs · [Tell Google about localized versions of your page](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/localized-versions) · Used by `DEV-INT-07`, the glossary term *hreflang*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google determines a page's language for indexing from the page content, not from a language code in the URL.

- **[Stage]** Google annotates each page with only one language in the index.
  <br><sub>`D2-C586` · Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Pages that mix several languages make it very hard for Google to decide which language a page is in, so each page should make its target language obvious and avoid mixing languages.
  <br><sub>`D2-C587` · Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation (Google) · confirmed by Google docs · [Managing multi-regional and multilingual sites](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/managing-multi-regional-sites), [How Google knows what language to show in search results](https://support.google.com/websearch/answer/13511324?hl=en) · Used by `DEV-INT-07`</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's hreflang guide says pages that translate only the template (navigation, footer) around main content in one language still count as duplicates, because localized versions are duplicates only if the main content stays untranslated; it recommends hreflang for such pages.
  <br><sub>`D2-C589` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation · is the documentation · [Tell Google about localized versions of your page](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/localized-versions) · Used by `DEV-INT-07`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Because Google reads a page's language from its content and stores one language per page, translate templates (navigation, footer, buttons, legal notices) together with the main text; large untranslated blocks risk the page being annotated with the wrong language.

- **[Docs]** Google's spam policies define scaled content abuse as generating many pages mainly to manipulate rankings, with little or no value to users, no matter how they are created, and list automated translating of scraped content among the examples.

- **[Analysis]** Treat machine translation as a first draft: have a native speaker review it and adapt dates, calendars and units before publishing, because unreviewed bulk translation that adds little value can also fall under Google's scaled content abuse policy.

  <br><sub>`D2-C614` · Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation (Google) · not in Google docs · Extended by [D3-C341](D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** According to consumer data shown on a slide in the talk (source not captured), German shoppers also rely heavily on expert recommendations and certifications when judging product quality.
  <br><sub>`D2-C615` · Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** According to consumer data shown on a slide in the talk (source not captured), French shoppers particularly want to know where a product comes from.
  <br><sub>`D2-C616` · Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Localise the trust signals on product pages, not only the words: if the findings shown hold for your category, lead with reviews in the US, brand reputation elsewhere in Europe, expert certifications in Germany and origin information in France, and test the order per market.
  <br><sub>`D2-C617` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's hreflang guide says the ISO 639-1 language code can be followed by a script in ISO 15924 format, such as zh-Hant or zh-Hans, and by an optional ISO 3166-1 Alpha-2 region code, as in zh-Hans-US.
  <br><sub>`D2-C830` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation · is the documentation · [Tell Google about localized versions of your page](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/localized-versions) · Used by `DEV-INT-04`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google said that working out a site's localized pages and which countries it targets is one of the difficult, complex tasks for it in indexing.
  <br><sub>`D2-C961` · Day 2, Focusing on Internationalisation and Localisation (Google)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google said incorrect hreflang language or region codes are a mistake it finds very often, with the same wrong codes coming up again and again, especially in Europe, because site owners assume the codes are easy.
